Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio of Correlations (HTMT)

Source: R/htmt.R
htmt.Rd

Computes the HTMT discriminant-validity index of Henseler, Ringle, and Sarstedt (2015) for every pair of constructs: the average correlation between items of different constructs, divided by the geometric mean of the average correlations among items within each construct. Two constructs whose HTMT approaches 1 are empirically indistinguishable however cleanly the model draws them; the customary red flags are 0.85 (strict) or 0.90 (liberal). An optional bootstrap gives a one-sided upper confidence bound, the quantity actually compared against the cutoff in the validity literature.

Usage

htmt(data, blocks, B = 0, conf_level = 0.95, seed = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data.frame of item responses.

blocks

Named list of character vectors: each element names a construct and gives its item columns (two or more per construct, two or more constructs). The blocks are disjoint: each item is listed once, in one block, and each construct has a name of its own (see Disjoint blocks under Details).

B

Number of bootstrap resamples for the upper confidence bound, a single whole number; 0 (default) skips the bootstrap and reports the point estimates only. When positive it must be at least 200 at the default conf_level (100 at 0.90, 1000 at 0.99): the bound is one quantile of the resamples, reported only when at least 10 of them lie beyond it and never from fewer than 100. A smaller positive B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). See Bootstrap replications under Details and dmar_bootstrap.

conf_level

Confidence level for the one-sided upper bound. Defaults to 0.95.

seed

Optional integer seed for the bootstrap, used locally (the caller's random number generator state is restored on exit).

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with one row per construct pair and the same four columns whatever B: construct_1, construct_2, htmt, and ci_upper, the one-sided conf_level bootstrap percentile bound, which is NA when B = 0 (no bootstrap was run). Both are NA for a pair whose ratio is undefined on the data (see Details). With B > 0 the table also carries the attributes conf_level, B (requested), B_used (the number of resamples the bound was computed from), n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status (see Bootstrap replications under Details).

Details

All correlations are Pearson, computed on pairwise-complete observations, and every one of them enters its average as an absolute value, the monotrait correlations among the items of a block as well as the heterotrait correlations between blocks. This is the ratio of arithmetic means that semTools' htmt() computes with htmt2 = FALSE and its default absolute = TRUE; on incomplete data the two agree only when semTools is given the same pairwise-complete correlations (through its sample.cov argument), since by default it deletes incomplete rows listwise, and its missing = "pairwise" option estimates the correlations through lavaan, whose values differ from stats::cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs"). Absolute values make the ratio indifferent to the direction in which an item is keyed, since reversing an item changes the signs of its correlations and not their sizes. With signed correlations, a reverse keyed item that was not recoded lowers its block's average within-construct correlation, which raises the ratio, while its negative correlations with the items of the other block partly cancel the positive ones in the numerator, so the ratio would depend on how the items happen to be scored. Values near or above 1 indicate that the two item sets correlate across constructs about as strongly as within them. HTMT is a correlation-based screen, deliberately model-free; the confirmatory companion is the latent correlation between the two factors (see correction_for_attenuation and its factor-model discussion, and the phi rows of fa_confirmatory with output = "measurement").

Disjoint blocks. The ratio compares two sets of items, so the blocks are disjoint sets of distinct items under distinct names. An item listed twice in one block would enter that block's average with its correlation of 1 with itself, and its other correlations would be counted twice; an item placed in two blocks would enter the average correlation between them with its correlation of 1 with itself; and two blocks under one name could not be told apart. Each of these, and an item whose name belongs to two or more columns of data, is refused with an error of class dmar_htmt_blocks_invalid (see dmar_metadata) before any correlation is computed or any resample drawn, whatever B. The condition's reason element names the check that failed ("construct_names", "repeated", "shared", or "data_names"), and its blocks and items elements the names at issue. A ratio for item sets that overlap would be a different quantity, which this function does not compute.

A pair's ratio is undefined when a correlation it averages cannot be computed: an item with no variance, or two items never observed together, as in a planned missing data design whose forms give the items of two blocks to different respondents. That pair's htmt (and ci_upper) is NA, with a warning that names it, and the other pairs are reported; the call stops only when no pair is defined.

The bootstrap, when requested (B > 0), resamples the rows of data with replacement B times and recomputes every pairwise HTMT on each resample; the reported ci_upper is the conf_level empirical quantile of each pair's bootstrap distribution, a one-sided upper percentile bound (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). That bound is the only interval offered, matching how the validity literature uses HTMT (the question is whether the ratio credibly exceeds the cutoff); no two-sided or bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) variant is provided. The ratio of each resample is the one reported, with every correlation an absolute value, so a resample that draws a negative correlation within a block enters with its size. Bootstrap results vary from run to run; supply seed for reproducibility.

Bootstrap replications. The bound of each pair is the conf_level quantile of its B resampled ratios, so it is run only when B puts at least 10 resamples beyond it (200 at the 95 percent level). A replication in which the HTMT of some pair defined on the data is undefined (an item that is constant in the resample, or two items never observed together) is dropped and counted, never replaced, and the bound is computed from the rest. The result records B (requested), B_used (the number the bound rests on), n_dropped, and B_required (the fewest replications a request may ask for; that count is held to B, not to B_used) as attributes, with bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share"). One warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped states the counts when any replication was dropped, with a caution when the dropped replications are at least the 5 percent of B that lies beyond one limit at the 95 percent level, because they could then decide by themselves where that limit falls. When more than half were dropped, the bound of every pair is NA, the estimate is returned, and the warning has class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a smaller B (2 or more) run for a first look or a demonstration; every such call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory and the result is not one to report. See dmar_bootstrap for the rule and its reasons.

References

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 43(1), 115–135. doi:10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8

average_variance_extracted for the convergent side of the validity ledger; reliability_omega for the composite reliability of each block; correction_for_attenuation for the latent correlation route.

Examples

# Two clean constructs and their six items.
set.seed(113)
n <- 300
f1 <- rnorm(n); f2 <- 0.3 * f1 + sqrt(1 - 0.09) * rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(
  a1 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6), a2 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
  a3 = .6 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .8),
  b1 = .8 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .6), b2 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
  b3 = .6 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .8))
h <- htmt(d, blocks = list(A = c("a1", "a2", "a3"),
                           B = c("b1", "b2", "b3")))
h
#>  construct_1 construct_2 htmt  ci_upper
#>  A           B           0.269 <NA>    

# The broom verbs: one row per construct pair.
generics::tidy(h)
#>   term  estimate ci_upper
#> 1  A:B 0.2691979       NA
generics::glance(h)
#>   n_terms conf_level B_used
#> 1       1         NA     NA

# The upper confidence bound, which is the quantity the validity
# literature compares against 0.85 or 0.90, comes from a bootstrap
# that recomputes every pairwise ratio on each of B resamples and
# fills the ci_upper column, NA above. B = 500 keeps the example
# quick; a claim about discriminant validity deserves the bound at
# B = 10000 rather than the point estimate alone.
htmt(d, blocks = list(A = c("a1", "a2", "a3"),
                      B = c("b1", "b2", "b3")),
     B = 500, seed = 113)
#>  construct_1 construct_2 htmt  ci_upper
#>  A           B           0.269 0.378   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 500 replications, 500 used (0 dropped; at least 200 must be requested)
